Include clearly labeled CPU, memory, storage, GPU, input, output, and network components, with directional connectors that distinguish data, instructions, and control signals. Establish a strong title, legend, grouping, and visual hierarchy so the architecture can be understood at a glance. history.critique: Brief & Intent: The figure fails its own headline promise. The header claims '7 core' components and '3 types' of signals, but (a) the Network node is clipped by the bottom edge of the dark canvas — only the top of the wifi icon is visible, with no label, badge, or zone content, so the NETWORK zone is effectively empty; and (b) no green 'Instructions' edges exist anywhere in the diagram despite the legend defining them and the subtitle centering the piece on three signal kinds — only blue data and orange control are drawn, so the core brief requirement (distinguish data, instructions, control) is only half met. Grouping is asserted but untrue: the dashed zone labeled COMPUTE encloses Input (an I/O device) and the MEMORY zone encloses Output (I/O), directly contradicting the sidebar's four-group system (Compute/Memory/I/O/Network). Clarity & Hierarchy: Two conflicting numbering schemes coexist — sidebar groups are 01–04 while node badges run 01–06 with mixed tags (CPU is '02 · COMPUTE' but the sidebar's '02' is Memory), so the same token means different things in adjacent panels. Edge semantics are ambiguous: the vertical orange line along CPU's left edge has no label or arrowhead; 'requests' floats beside two candidate edges (CPU→Output and Memory→CPU) with no clear referent; the 'address-bus · control' label sits on top of its own dashes and collides with neighboring text. The legend's control swatch is dashed, but the figure's vertical control line is solid, so the diagram language is not self-consistent; the Inspector card is an empty placeholder in the default state. Visual System & Craft: The SVG content overflows its viewBox at the bottom (hard clipping = jank) while the left/right of the panel hold large dead zones — the layout is simultaneously sparse and overflowing. The CPU node is taller than its peers, breaking the otherwise regular grid; connector labels are placed on the stroke rather than offset from it; arrowhead usage is inconsistent. Expressiveness: The dark schematic panel, monospace labels, figure metadata, and the blue-accented title give a genuinely good technical identity, but the diagram itself reads as a generic two-row block diagram; the mislabeled zones and the missing instruction layer flatten the 'three-signal anatomy' idea that is the piece's distinctive, memorable claim. Real trade-offs: adding instruction edges raises density (must be capped and routed through existing channels); restructuring into true quadrant zones breaks the current tidy two-row grid and lengthens some connectors (acceptable, because grouping truthfulness is a brief requirement and quadrants improve at-a-glance reading); unifying numbering requires re-badging every node (cheap, high payoff).
history.suggestion: One prioritized plan, in order: 1) Complete and unclip the figure — resize the SVG viewBox/panel so all seven nodes render fully, and give Network a proper node (icon, label, badge) inside a real Network zone; this restores the '7 core' claim and removes the only hard jank. 2) Add the missing instruction layer — draw exactly two green dashed edges with arrowheads and labels, Memory→CPU 'fetch' and CPU→GPU 'program', so all three legend types are present; cap total edges at ~9 to keep the restrained color coding legible. 3) Rebuild zones as four true quadrants matching the GROUPINGS card — Compute (CPU, GPU), Memory (Memory, Storage), I/O (Input, Output), Network (Network) — tag zones 01–04 to match the sidebar, and switch node badges to group-prefixed IDs (C1, C2, M1, M2, IO1, IO2, N1) to eliminate the dual-numbering conflict. 4) Enforce one diagram language — data = solid blue, instructions = green dashed, control = orange dashed everywhere (convert or remove the solid orange CPU line), consistent arrowheads, all labels offset from their strokes with a small gap (no text on dashes), and assign 'requests' to a single specific edge (e.g., relabel the CPU→Output edge 'results'). 5) Craft pass — equalize node heights, snap everything to a shared grid, tighten the panel to its content to kill the dead space, and wire the promised hover states (node role, edge signal) so the Inspector card populates instead of sitting empty. This preserves all required content, makes the three-signal story the focal moment, and keeps the existing dark-schematic identity intact.

- Brief & Intent Alignment: requested content, relationships, atmosphere, and intended experience are visibly and substantively fulfilled; polish never excuses omission.
- Clarity & Information Hierarchy: focal priority, grouping, reading flow, states, and controls are immediately understandable.
- Visual System & Craft: geometry, palette, typography, spacing, components, and details form one precise production-quality system without clipping or jank.

Create a single-page SVG infographic of a computer system and the information moving through it. Put strong emphasis on information clarity, consistent diagram language, precise alignment, restrained color coding, and professional technical polish.

Respect the offline self-contained HTML constraint; never request external libraries or assets.

history.critique: The single dominant failure is that the primary deliverable is missing: the large dark canvas on the left — the element that should contain the SVG architecture — is an empty faint grid with zero components and zero connectors. The brief's core requirement (labeled CPU, memory, storage, GPU, input, output, network blocks plus directional data/instruction/control connectors) is entirely unmet, so the artifact is a frame without the picture. This cascades across all four pressures. (1) Brief & Intent: the legend describes three signal types and the groupings card lists four groups, but there is nothing in the diagram to apply them to; the '7 core components' metadata claim is unverifiable; the inspector promises 'hover a component / hover a connector' interactions on objects that do not exist. (2) Clarity & Hierarchy: focal priority is inverted — the biggest visual mass (the void) is the supposed focal point, so the eye lands on the right-rail reference cards (legend/groupings), which are secondary material, making the page read as a spec sheet rather than a diagram. The top-right metadata block (SCALE/VIEW/SIGNALS/COMPONENTS) is dense and low-contrast, competing with the title for the top zone. (3) Visual System & Craft: the chrome is genuinely strong and consistent (monospace eyebrow, FIG. 01, rounded cards, restrained blue/green/orange coding, dashed inspector box), but the empty dark panel reads as a rendering bug or placeholder, not a deliberate choice; the grid is so faint it looks like noise; and the Inspector card is clipped at the bottom edge ('Hover a connector to read its signal.' is cut off), a real jank/clipping defect. The right column is also much shorter than the left, leaving awkward imbalance. (4) Expressiveness & Distinctiveness: the 'technical blueprint / systems doc' identity is appropriate and the typography gives it character, but with no architecture drawn there is no memorable moment or authored originality — all expression lives in the frame. Real trade-offs: the dark canvas is the right call for making glowing signal lines pop, but empty it looks broken, so it must be populated to become a feature; the interactive 'inspector' over-promises for a single-page at-a-glance infographic, so interactivity must either be implemented (self-contained CSS :hover) or downgraded to a static reading guide; and the three-signal color system is good and should stay restrained, meaning component fills must remain neutral so the signal colors carry all the meaning rather than adding a fourth color per component.
